paper.title: Taxation and the long run allocation of labor: Theory and Danish evidence
paper.code_data_availability: No data availability statement and no Statistics Denmark project reference is given. …

registers.name_in_paper: the Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA)
registers.role: sample frame, linkage, treatment input (workplace average hourly wage rates and the offered wage distribution P) and outcome (the number of stayers x_h out of n_h employees)
variables_mentioned: average wage rate of the employees of the workplace
number of 'stayers' (employed at the workplace in 2005 and still employed at it in 2006)
number of 'new hires' (employed at the workplace in 2005 but not in 2004)
number of 'new hires from non-employment' (employed at the workplace in 2005 but not employed at any workplace in 2004)
annual labor income (including mandatory pension fund payments)

registers.name_in_paper: the Wage Statistics Register (WSR or Lønstatistikken)
registers.role: robustness: an alternative employer-reported hourly wage rate accounting for overtime and part-time work, used to impute an adjusted wage rate
variables_mentioned: hourly wage rate per hour reported by employers

registers.role: variable construction: annual labor income, the numerator of the hourly wage rate; the Danish Tax Agency obtains third-party information from employers on nearly all labor income
variable construction: annual hours are imputed from ATP payments, which depend on the number of hours worked

linkages: Workers and workplaces are linked and uniquely identified over time in IDA, so that worker transitions in and out of the workplace may be tracked; in a specific week of each of 2004, 2005 and 2006 the paper knows which workers were employed at each workplace
Each worker is associated with the average hourly wage rate of his workplace, which stands for the wage w_i of job i in the model

IDA wage rates are linked at worker level to Wage Statistics Register hourly wage rates for the 60% of workers with a reported WSR wage, in order to estimate E(w_WSR | w_IDA) and impute an adjusted wage rate for the full sample
Hourly wage rates are linked to the effective marginal tax rate schedule of Kleven and Kreiner (2006) by converting them into annual labor income using median annual hours (1660 h)

sample.universe: The full population of workers and workplaces in Denmark for the years 2004-2006
sample.unit_of_observation: Workplace (an establishment defined by a geographical location) observed in 2005, with its number of employees n_h and its number of stayers x_h from 2005 to 2006
selection_rules: Employed in private sector workplaces in 2005
Workplace average wage rates in the top percentile of the wage distribution (wage rates above DKK 714) excluded, to reduce the impact of potential measurement error in workplace average wages
Wage rates below DKK 90 dropped (the cut-off w1 of DKK 90 corresponds approximately to the sector-level minimum wage floor in 2005; alternatives of DKK 80 and DKK 100 are used in robustness)
Low-wage job offers that would never be accepted are disregarded, and w1 - T1 >= w0 - T0 is assumed

For the WSR robustness only: the top and bottom one percent of IDA wage observations are dropped, as are IDA wage rates deemed of low quality by Statistics Denmark, leaving 54% of the original sample of workers
sample.period: 2004-2006, with 2005 as the base sample year and the 2006 Danish tax system (deflated to 2005) as the initial tax system
sample.n_individuals: 1.4 million workers with an observed IDA wage rate (60% of them also have a reported WSR wage rate)

construction_notes: The wage rate of a worker is annual labor income (including mandatory pension fund payments) divided by annual hours; each worker is then assigned his workplace's average hourly wage rate, because it is the firm component in wages that matters for job-to-job mobility in on-the-job search models
Average workplace characteristics in the final sample: size 11.0 employees, stayers 7.7, wage DKK 197.6, new hires 3.3, of which 0.6 from non-employment (Table 1)

Effective marginal tax rates come from the empirical 2006 Danish tax function of Kleven and Kreiner (2006) - income taxes, indirect taxes and the marginal claw-back on benefits - deflated by the overall growth rate in average annual labor income between 2005 and 2006

Hourly wage rates are converted into annual labor incomes by multiplying by the median annual hours worked in the data (1660 h), so that an effective marginal tax rate is assigned to each hourly wage from DKK 90 to DKK 714 (these are m1,...,mN; Fig. 1)
The tax-benefit function is built from the marginal tax rates by choosing T0 arbitrarily and setting T1 = T0 + m0 w1 and T(i+1) = Ti + mi(w(i+1) - wi) for i = 1,...,N-1

The participation tax is set to m0 = 0.59 in the baseline (the marginal tax rate at the lowest wages, around DKK 90), with m0 = 0.82 in robustness; w0 = (1 - m0) w1 = 36.9 follows from the indifference condition

The offered wage distribution P is the distribution of firm-specific average wages for persons entering firms in 2005 from non-employment in 2004, each firm's wage weighted by its share of all workers hired from non-employment

Robustness: an overtime/part-time adjusted wage rate is imputed from the fractional polynomial E(w_WSR | w_IDA) = 215.7 + 37.9[(w_IDA/100)^2 - 5.1] - 13.7[(w_IDA/100)^2 ln(w_IDA/100) - 4.1], then averaged within workplaces and used in place of the IDA wage
Robustness: an alternative 'data job destruction rate' q*delta is allowed, so that the observed separation rate is d'_h = q*delta + lambda s_h (1 - P_h) (Eq. (19)) with q = 1, 3, 6

claims.statement: In the estimated structural on-the-job search model, alpha is 0.0098 (Table 2, point estimate).

treatment.label: alpha, the composite job-offer-arrival and search-cost parameter of the on-the-job search model

register_source.value: Model parameter; estimated from IDA workplace stayer counts 2005-2006

definition.value: alpha = lambda^(1+1/gamma)/c_0, where lambda is the parameter of the Poisson frequency lambda s_i at which a worker in state i receives job offers and c_0 is the scale of the isoelastic mobility effort cost function c(s) = c_0 s^(1+1/gamma)/(1+1/gamma). It enters Eq. (16), which determines the optimal search intensities lambda s_i recursively from lambda s_N = 0.

timing.value: Long run steady state of the model; the estimation uses the one-year transition from 2005 to 2006 and the 2006 tax system

outcome.label: x_h, the number of 'stayers' at workplace h

register_source.value: IDA (Integrated Database for Labour Market Research), Statistics Denmark; workplace-level counts of employees and stayers 2005-2006

definition.value: The number of workers employed at workplace h in 2005 who are still employed at it in 2006, out of the n_h employees registered at the workplace in 2005. Given the separation rate d_h = delta + lambda s_h (1 - P_h), the probability of x stayers is binomial with staying probability exp(-d_h); the product of these probabilities over all workplaces is the likelihood maximised to estimate (alpha, delta, gamma).

timing.value: Employment status in a specific week of 2005 and of 2006

units.value: model units: dimensionless parameter of the search technology / cost function

estimand.target_population: The representative worker of the model, taken to stand for workers aged 18-65 employed in private sector workplaces in Denmark in 2005 (all workers are assumed identical)
estimand.time_horizon: Long run steady state of the model; the estimation uses the one-year transition from 2005 to 2006 and the 2006 tax system

population.description: The representative worker of the estimated on-the-job search model, calibrated on the full population of workers and workplaces in Denmark 2004-2006: workers aged 18-65 employed in private sector workplaces in 2005, aggregated to 126,400 workplaces employing 1.4 million workers.
population.period: 2004-2006 (base year 2005; the 2006 Danish effective marginal tax schedule deflated to 2005)
subgroups_defined: students (removed in one robustness specification)
individuals older than 50 (removed in one robustness specification)
workers with less than 1 year of work experience (removed in one robustness test)
closing plants, and closing plus downsizing plants (removed in robustness tests)
men
women
population.selection: Workplace-level sample drawn from IDA: private sector workplaces in Denmark with workers aged 18-65 in 2005, observed in a specific week of 2004, 2005 and 2006. Observations in the top percentile of the wage distribution (wage rates above DKK 714) are excluded and wage rates below DKK 90 are dropped. 126,400 workplaces remain.

identification.source_of_variation: No reform or experiment: the structural parameters are identified from cross-sectional variation across 126,400 Danish private-sector workplaces in 2005 in the number of stayers x_h out of n_h employees (the 2005-to-2006 separation rate), combined with the exogenous effective marginal tax schedule of the Danish 2006 tax system (Kleven and Kreiner, 2006) mapped onto workplace average hourly wage rates, and with the offered wage distribution P estimated from workers hired from non-employment. The authors state the analysis 'exploits only cross-sectional variation across individuals for identification'.

key_assumptions.assumption: Worker and firm components in the wage are independent, so that a workplace's average wage rate measures the firm wage component plus noise and can be used as the wage w_i of job i in the model
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted, not tested; the authors restate it in the concluding section as one of the two things 'the empirical identification relies on'. No balance or decomposition evidence is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The distribution of job opportunities (the offered wage distribution P and its domain) is exogenous: it is not affected by taxation or by workers' search behaviour
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted; footnote 11 states that P and its domain are exogenous and can only be observed for the existing w1. No test.

key_assumptions.assumption: All workers are identical: the underlying (offered) wage distribution is the same for every individual, so there is no ability heterogeneity
key_assumptions.supported_by: Conceded in the concluding section as 'the most heroic assumption of the model'; not relaxed or tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Workers are indifferent between the lowest wage job and non-employment, w1 - T1 = w0 - T0, which pins down the value of leisure/home production w0 = (1 - m0) w1 = 36.9
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed as an identifying restriction; the implied value DKK 36.9 per hour is reported but not validated externally.

formal.as_written: w1 − T1 ≥ w0 − T0 ... w1 − T1 = w0 − T0, which implies w0 = w1 − (T1 − T0) = (1 − m0) w1

key_assumptions.assumption: The mobility (search) effort cost function is isoelastic, c(s) = c0 s^(1+1/gamma)/(1+1/gamma)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed 'to identify the model' (Eq. (15)); no specification test of the cost function is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: No discounting, so only the long run steady state matters for welfare and for the evaluation of tax reforms
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a simplifying modelling assumption in Section 2; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Job destruction is exogenous and random, arriving at a constant Poisson rate delta that does not depend on the worker's search effort or wage
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a model primitive; probed indirectly by the alternative-q robustness in Table 4 and by removing closing plants in Table 5.

key_assumptions.assumption: The offered wage distribution P is identified by the distribution of firm-specific average wages of workers who entered firms in 2005 from non-employment in 2004, weighted by each firm's share of such hires
key_assumptions.supported_by: Follows Christensen et al. (2005); supported only by the model-consistent observation that the earned wage distribution stochastically dominates it (Fig. 2).

threats_discussed: Measurement error in annual hours (imputed from the ATP mandatory pension fund; overtime not accounted for, part-time hours imprecise), hence in the hourly wage rate - addressed by imputing a WSR-based adjusted wage rate
Part of the observed job destruction may be measurement error rather than 'true' job destruction, inflating delta and the implied non-employment rate - addressed by the alternative-q experiments
Entry-exit behaviour of students and of workers above 50 (retirement) may drive the separation rate
Closing and downsizing plants may drive the job destruction rate
The choice of the bottom cut-off wage rate w1 and of the participation tax m0
robustness_checks: Alternative values of the data-to-true job destruction ratio q = 1, 3, 6 with the full estimation and the tax experiment redone (Table 4)
IDA wage rate replaced by a WSR (Lonstatistikken) overtime/part-time adjusted wage rate imputed from a fractional polynomial regression (Table 5, column 'Adjusted wage rate')
Students excluded; individuals older than 50 excluded (Table 5)
Closing plants excluded; closing plus downsizing plants excluded
Workers with less than 1 year of work experience excluded
Alternative bottom cut-off wage rates w1 = DKK 80 and DKK 100 (Table 5)
Participation tax m0 = 0.82 instead of 0.59 (Table 5)
Separate estimation for men and women (footnote 17)
Elasticity recomputed from the linear-tax formula Eq. (12) as a check on the non-linear computation
Smaller relative changes in the net-of-tax rate, which 'lead to almost the same elasticity estimate' (footnote 12)
unresolved_confounders: Worker heterogeneity: all workers are assumed identical, so the underlying wage distribution is identical for all individuals ('the most heroic assumption of the model')
Mobility motives other than wages: geographical moves, house purchases, and voluntary moves to lower-paid jobs are not modelled
Within-firm promotions leading to discrete earnings jumps are not accounted for
Only cross-sectional variation across individuals is exploited for identification

estimator.value: Maximum likelihood estimation of a structural on-the-job search model: the triplet (alpha, delta, gamma) is estimated by maximising the log likelihood of the observed number of stayers x_h out of n_h employees per workplace (binomial, staying probability exp(-d_h)), taking into account the functional relationship from (alpha, delta, gamma) to the separation rates d_h

estimation.specification: Eq. (16) solved recursively from lambda s_N = 0 for the optimal search intensities, Eq. (17) for the separation rates d_h = delta + lambda s_h (1 - P_h), isoelastic cost function Eq. (15); the offered wage distribution P, the tax function T and the wage grid w_i are held fixed. Baseline specification: q = 1, m_0 = 0.59, w_1 = DKK 90, IDA hourly wage rates.
estimation.weights: The offered wage distribution P_i is constructed by weighting the firm-specific wage of firm i by the fraction of all workers hired from non-employment by firm i

sample_n.value: 126,400 workplaces (employing in total 1.4 million workers with an observed IDA wage rate)

source_table.value: Table 2, row alpha, Point estimate and Standard error columns

ambiguities: Polarity of the outcome x_h (number of stayers) is set relative to the concept the paper measures with it - job separation / labor mobility - so more stayers is less of that concept.
Table 4 column q = 1 reprints the same baseline estimate (0.0098); it is not extracted again as a separate claim.

value.equation_number: unnumbered log likelihood on p. 79, with Eqs. (15), (16) and (17)
value.as_printed: L(α, δ, γ) = Π_{h=1}^{H} [ C(n_h, x_h) e^{-d_h x} (1 - e^{-d_h})^{n_h - x} ] ; ln L(α, δ, γ) = Σ_{h=1}^{N} [ ln C(n_h, x_h) - d_h x + (n_h - x) ln(1 - e^{-d_h}) ], where d_h = δ + λ s_h (1 - P_h) depends directly on δ and, through λ s_h, on (α, δ, γ)
value.normalisation: λ s_N = 0 (no search in the highest-wage job); w_1 = DKK 90 and w_0 = (1 - m_0) w_1 = 36.9 with m_0 = 0.59; T_0 chosen arbitrarily with T_1 = T_0 + m_0 w_1 and T_{i+1} = T_i + m_i (w_{i+1} - w_i); hourly wages converted to annual income using median annual hours 1660

theory_referenced: On-the-job search / job ladder model of labor mobility (Burdett, 1978; Christensen et al., 2005)

prior_findings_compared.as_stated: The parameter estimates are close to the findings of Christensen et al. (2005).

outcomes_examined_not_reported: Confidence intervals of the further estimations (e.g. of the elasticity) - stated to be very narrow but not reported
Standard errors for the alternative specifications of Tables 4 and 5 - stated to be very small and not reported

identification.source_of_variation: No reform or experiment: the structural parameters are identified from cross-sectional variation across 126,400 Danish private-sector workplaces in 2005 in the number of stayers x_h out of n_h employees (the 2005-to-2006 separation rate), combined with the exogenous effective marginal tax schedule of the Danish 2006 tax system (Kleven and Kreiner, 2006) mapped onto workplace average hourly wage rates, and with the offered wage distribution P estimated from workers hired from non-employment. key_assumptions.supported_by: Conceded in the concluding section as 'the most heroic assumption of the model'; not relaxed or tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Workers are indifferent between the lowest wage job and non-employment, w1 - T1 = w0 - T0, which pins down the value of leisure/home production w0 = (1 - m0) w1 = 36.9

formal.as_written: w1 − T1 ≥ w0 − T0 ... w1 − T1 = w0 − T0, which implies w0 = w1 − (T1 − T0) = (1 − m0) w1

key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed 'to identify the model' (Eq. (15)); no specification test of the cost function is reported.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a simplifying modelling assumption in Section 2; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Job destruction is exogenous and random, arriving at a constant Poisson rate delta that does not depend on the worker's search effort or wage
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a model primitive; probed indirectly by the alternative-q robustness in Table 4 and by removing closing plants in Table 5.

estimation.specification: Eq. (16) solved recursively from lambda s_N = 0 for the optimal search intensities, Eq. population.selection: Workplace-level sample drawn from IDA: private sector workplaces in Denmark with workers aged 18-65 in 2005, observed in a specific week of 2004, 2005 and 2006. Observations in the top percentile of the wage distribution (wage rates above DKK 714) are excluded and wage rates below DKK 90 are dropped. 126,400 workplaces remain. For this specification the IDA wage sample is first trimmed (top and bottom one percent dropped, plus IDA wage rates deemed of low quality by Statistics Denmark, leaving 54% of the original worker sample) to estimate the WSR-IDA wage relationship, which is then used to impute an adjusted wage rate for the full sample.

identification.source_of_variation: No reform or experiment: the structural parameters are identified from cross-sectional variation across 126,400 Danish private-sector workplaces in 2005 in the number of stayers x_h out of n_h employees (the 2005-to-2006 separation rate), combined with the exogenous effective marginal tax schedule of the Danish 2006 tax system (Kleven and Kreiner, 2006) mapped onto workplace average hourly wage rates, and with the offered wage distribution P estimated from workers hired from non-employment. The authors state the analysis 'exploits only cross-sectional variation across individuals for identification'.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted, not tested; the authors restate it in the concluding section as one of the two things 'the empirical identification relies on'. No balance or decomposition evidence is offered.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted; footnote 11 states that P and its domain are exogenous and can only be observed for the existing w1. No test.

key_assumptions.assumption: All workers are identical: the underlying (offered) wage distribution is the same for every individual, so there is no ability heterogeneity
key_assumptions.supported_by: Conceded in the concluding section as 'the most heroic assumption of the model'; not relaxed or tested.

definition.value: The number of workers employed at workplace h in 2005 who are still employed at it in 2006, out of the n_h employees registered at the workplace in 2005. population.selection: Workplace-level sample drawn from IDA: private sector workplaces in Denmark with workers aged 18-65 in 2005. Observations in the top percentile of the wage distribution (wage rates above DKK 714) are excluded; the bottom cut-off is set at DKK 100 instead of DKK 90.

identification.source_of_variation: No reform or experiment: the structural parameters are identified from cross-sectional variation across 126,400 Danish private-sector workplaces in 2005 in the number of stayers x_h out of n_h employees (the 2005-to-2006 separation rate), combined with the exogenous effective marginal tax schedule of the Danish 2006 tax system (Kleven and Kreiner, 2006) mapped onto workplace average hourly wage rates, and with the offered wage distribution P estimated from workers hired from non-employment. The authors state the analysis 'exploits only cross-sectional variation across individuals for identification'.

key_assumptions.assumption: Worker and firm components in the wage are independent, so that a workplace's average wage rate measures the firm wage component plus noise and can be used as the wage w_i of job i in the model
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted, not tested; the authors restate it in the concluding section as one of the two things 'the empirical identification relies on'. No balance or decomposition evidence is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The distribution of job opportunities (the offered wage distribution P and its domain) is exogenous: it is not affected by taxation or by workers' search behaviour
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted; footnote 11 states that P and its domain are exogenous and can only be observed for the existing w1. No test.

key_assumptions.assumption: All workers are identical: the underlying (offered) wage distribution is the same for every individual, so there is no ability heterogeneity
key_assumptions.supported_by: Conceded in the concluding section as 'the most heroic assumption of the model'; not relaxed or tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Workers are indifferent between the lowest wage job and non-employment, w1 - T1 = w0 - T0, which pins down the value of leisure/home production w0 = (1 - m0) w1 = 36.9
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed as an identifying restriction; the implied value DKK 36.9 per hour is reported but not validated externally.

formal.as_written: w1 − T1 ≥ w0 − T0 ... w1 − T1 = w0 − T0, which implies w0 = w1 − (T1 − T0) = (1 − m0) w1

key_assumptions.assumption: The mobility (search) effort cost function is isoelastic, c(s) = c0 s^(1+1/gamma)/(1+1/gamma)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed 'to identify the model' (Eq. (15)); no specification test of the cost function is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: No discounting, so only the long run steady state matters for welfare and for the evaluation of tax reforms
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a simplifying modelling assumption in Section 2; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Job destruction is exogenous and random, arriving at a constant Poisson rate delta that does not depend on the worker's search effort or wage
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a model primitive; probed indirectly by the alternative-q robustness in Table 4 and by removing closing plants in Table 5.

key_assumptions.assumption: The offered wage distribution P is identified by the distribution of firm-specific average wages of workers who entered firms in 2005 from non-employment in 2004, weighted by each firm's share of such hires
key_assumptions.supported_by: Follows Christensen et al. (2005); supported only by the model-consistent observation that the earned wage distribution stochastically dominates it (Fig. 2).

estimation.specification: Eq. (16) solved recursively from lambda s_N = 0 for the optimal search intensities, Eq. population.selection: Workplace-level sample drawn from IDA: private sector workplaces in Denmark with workers aged 18-65 in 2005, observed in a specific week of 2004, 2005 and 2006. Observations in the top percentile of the wage distribution (wage rates above DKK 714) are excluded and wage rates below DKK 90 are dropped. 126,400 workplaces remain.

identification.source_of_variation: No reform or experiment: the structural parameters are identified from cross-sectional variation across 126,400 Danish private-sector workplaces in 2005 in the number of stayers x_h out of n_h employees (the 2005-to-2006 separation rate), combined with the exogenous effective marginal tax schedule of the Danish 2006 tax system (Kleven and Kreiner, 2006) mapped onto workplace average hourly wage rates, and with the offered wage distribution P estimated from workers hired from non-employment. The authors state the analysis 'exploits only cross-sectional variation across individuals for identification'.

key_assumptions.assumption: Worker and firm components in the wage are independent, so that a workplace's average wage rate measures the firm wage component plus noise and can be used as the wage w_i of job i in the model
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted, not tested; the authors restate it in the concluding section as one of the two things 'the empirical identification relies on'. No balance or decomposition evidence is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The distribution of job opportunities (the offered wage distribution P and its domain) is exogenous: it is not affected by taxation or by workers' search behaviour
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted; footnote 11 states that P and its domain are exogenous and can only be observed for the existing w1. No test.

key_assumptions.assumption: All workers are identical: the underlying (offered) wage distribution is the same for every individual, so there is no ability heterogeneity
key_assumptions.supported_by: Conceded in the concluding section as 'the most heroic assumption of the model'; not relaxed or tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Workers are indifferent between the lowest wage job and non-employment, w1 - T1 = w0 - T0, which pins down the value of leisure/home production w0 = (1 - m0) w1 = 36.9
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed as an identifying restriction; the implied value DKK 36.9 per hour is reported but not validated externally.

formal.as_written: w1 − T1 ≥ w0 − T0 ... w1 − T1 = w0 − T0, which implies w0 = w1 − (T1 − T0) = (1 − m0) w1

key_assumptions.assumption: The mobility (search) effort cost function is isoelastic, c(s) = c0 s^(1+1/gamma)/(1+1/gamma)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed 'to identify the model' (Eq. (15)); no specification test of the cost function is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: No discounting, so only the long run steady state matters for welfare and for the evaluation of tax reforms
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a simplifying modelling assumption in Section 2; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Job destruction is exogenous and random, arriving at a constant Poisson rate delta that does not depend on the worker's search effort or wage
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a model primitive; probed indirectly by the alternative-q robustness in Table 4 and by removing closing plants in Table 5.

key_assumptions.assumption: The offered wage distribution P is identified by the distribution of firm-specific average wages of workers who entered firms in 2005 from non-employment in 2004, weighted by each firm's share of such hires
key_assumptions.supported_by: Follows Christensen et al. (2005); supported only by the model-consistent observation that the earned wage distribution stochastically dominates it (Fig. 2).

key_assumptions.assumption: Behaviour depends on taxation only through the marginal tax rates, so the effective marginal tax rate schedule is sufficient information for estimation and for the policy simulations
key_assumptions.supported_by: Derived from Eq. (7) of the model: search effort depends on taxes only via T_{i+1} - T_i = m_i (w_{i+1} - w_i).

key_assumptions.assumption: The simulated reforms change only the intensive-margin marginal tax rates m1,...,mN-1: T0, T1 and hence w1 and the participation tax m0 are held fixed, and the offered wage distribution and the estimated structural parameters are invariant to the reform (no general-equilibrium wage response)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 4 and footnote 11 as 'an analytical necessity'; no general-equilibrium check is performed.

population.selection: Workplace-level sample drawn from IDA: private sector workplaces in Denmark with workers aged 18-65 in 2005, observed in a specific week of 2004, 2005 and 2006. Observations in the top percentile of the wage distribution (wage rates above DKK 714) are excluded and wage rates below DKK 90 are dropped. 126,400 workplaces remain. Students are removed.

identification.source_of_variation: No reform or experiment: the structural parameters are identified from cross-sectional variation across 126,400 Danish private-sector workplaces in 2005 in the number of stayers x_h out of n_h employees (the 2005-to-2006 separation rate), combined with the exogenous effective marginal tax schedule of the Danish 2006 tax system (Kleven and Kreiner, 2006) mapped onto workplace average hourly wage rates, and with the offered wage distribution P estimated from workers hired from non-employment. The authors state the analysis 'exploits only cross-sectional variation across individuals for identification'.

key_assumptions.assumption: Worker and firm components in the wage are independent, so that a workplace's average wage rate measures the firm wage component plus noise and can be used as the wage w_i of job i in the model
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted, not tested; the authors restate it in the concluding section as one of the two things 'the empirical identification relies on'. No balance or decomposition evidence is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The distribution of job opportunities (the offered wage distribution P and its domain) is exogenous: it is not affected by taxation or by workers' search behaviour
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted; footnote 11 states that P and its domain are exogenous and can only be observed for the existing w1. No test.

key_assumptions.assumption: All workers are identical: the underlying (offered) wage distribution is the same for every individual, so there is no ability heterogeneity
key_assumptions.supported_by: Conceded in the concluding section as 'the most heroic assumption of the model'; not relaxed or tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Workers are indifferent between the lowest wage job and non-employment, w1 - T1 = w0 - T0, which pins down the value of leisure/home production w0 = (1 - m0) w1 = 36.9
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed as an identifying restriction; the implied value DKK 36.9 per hour is reported but not validated externally.

formal.as_written: w1 − T1 ≥ w0 − T0 ... w1 − T1 = w0 − T0, which implies w0 = w1 − (T1 − T0) = (1 − m0) w1

key_assumptions.assumption: The mobility (search) effort cost function is isoelastic, c(s) = c0 s^(1+1/gamma)/(1+1/gamma)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed 'to identify the model' (Eq. (15)); no specification test of the cost function is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: No discounting, so only the long run steady state matters for welfare and for the evaluation of tax reforms
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a simplifying modelling assumption in Section 2; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Job destruction is exogenous and random, arriving at a constant Poisson rate delta that does not depend on the worker's search effort or wage
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a model primitive; probed indirectly by the alternative-q robustness in Table 4 and by removing closing plants in Table 5.

key_assumptions.assumption: The offered wage distribution P is identified by the distribution of firm-specific average wages of workers who entered firms in 2005 from non-employment in 2004, weighted by each firm's share of such hires
key_assumptions.supported_by: Follows Christensen et al. (2005); supported only by the model-consistent observation that the earned wage distribution stochastically dominates it (Fig. 2).

key_assumptions.assumption: Behaviour depends on taxation only through the marginal tax rates, so the effective marginal tax rate schedule is sufficient information for estimation and for the policy simulations
key_assumptions.supported_by: Derived from Eq. (7) of the model: search effort depends on taxes only via T_{i+1} - T_i = m_i (w_{i+1} - w_i).

key_assumptions.assumption: The simulated reforms change only the intensive-margin marginal tax rates m1,...,mN-1: T0, T1 and hence w1 and the participation tax m0 are held fixed, and the offered wage distribution and the estimated structural parameters are invariant to the reform (no general-equilibrium wage response)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 4 and footnote 11 as 'an analytical necessity'; no general-equilibrium check is performed.

population.selection: Workplace-level sample drawn from IDA: private sector workplaces in Denmark with workers aged 18-65 in 2005, observed in a specific week of 2004, 2005 and 2006. Observations in the top percentile of the wage distribution (wage rates above DKK 714) are excluded and wage rates below DKK 90 are dropped. 126,400 workplaces remain.

identification.source_of_variation: No reform or experiment: the structural parameters are identified from cross-sectional variation across 126,400 Danish private-sector workplaces in 2005 in the number of stayers x_h out of n_h employees (the 2005-to-2006 separation rate), combined with the exogenous effective marginal tax schedule of the Danish 2006 tax system (Kleven and Kreiner, 2006) mapped onto workplace average hourly wage rates, and with the offered wage distribution P estimated from workers hired from non-employment. The authors state the analysis 'exploits only cross-sectional variation across individuals for identification'.

key_assumptions.assumption: Worker and firm components in the wage are independent, so that a workplace's average wage rate measures the firm wage component plus noise and can be used as the wage w_i of job i in the model
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted, not tested; the authors restate it in the concluding section as one of the two things 'the empirical identification relies on'. No balance or decomposition evidence is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The distribution of job opportunities (the offered wage distribution P and its domain) is exogenous: it is not affected by taxation or by workers' search behaviour
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted; footnote 11 states that P and its domain are exogenous and can only be observed for the existing w1. No test.

key_assumptions.assumption: All workers are identical: the underlying (offered) wage distribution is the same for every individual, so there is no ability heterogeneity
key_assumptions.supported_by: Conceded in the concluding section as 'the most heroic assumption of the model'; not relaxed or tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Workers are indifferent between the lowest wage job and non-employment, w1 - T1 = w0 - T0, which pins down the value of leisure/home production w0 = (1 - m0) w1 = 36.9
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed as an identifying restriction; the implied value DKK 36.9 per hour is reported but not validated externally.

formal.as_written: w1 − T1 ≥ w0 − T0 ... w1 − T1 = w0 − T0, which implies w0 = w1 − (T1 − T0) = (1 − m0) w1

key_assumptions.assumption: The mobility (search) effort cost function is isoelastic, c(s) = c0 s^(1+1/gamma)/(1+1/gamma)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed 'to identify the model' (Eq. (15)); no specification test of the cost function is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: No discounting, so only the long run steady state matters for welfare and for the evaluation of tax reforms
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a simplifying modelling assumption in Section 2; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Job destruction is exogenous and random, arriving at a constant Poisson rate delta that does not depend on the worker's search effort or wage
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a model primitive; probed indirectly by the alternative-q robustness in Table 4 and by removing closing plants in Table 5.

key_assumptions.assumption: The offered wage distribution P is identified by the distribution of firm-specific average wages of workers who entered firms in 2005 from non-employment in 2004, weighted by each firm's share of such hires
key_assumptions.supported_by: Follows Christensen et al. (2005); supported only by the model-consistent observation that the earned wage distribution stochastically dominates it (Fig. 2).

key_assumptions.assumption: Behaviour depends on taxation only through the marginal tax rates, so the effective marginal tax rate schedule is sufficient information for estimation and for the policy simulations
key_assumptions.supported_by: Derived from Eq. (7) of the model: search effort depends on taxes only via T_{i+1} - T_i = m_i (w_{i+1} - w_i).

key_assumptions.assumption: The simulated reforms change only the intensive-margin marginal tax rates m1,...,mN-1: T0, T1 and hence w1 and the participation tax m0 are held fixed, and the offered wage distribution and the estimated structural parameters are invariant to the reform (no general-equilibrium wage response)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 4 and footnote 11 as 'an analytical necessity'; no general-equilibrium check is performed.

claims.statement: A small reduction in all marginal tax rates along the intensive margin yields a change in the excess burden of taxation equal to 0.94 of the mechanical loss in tax revenue (Table 5, column 'Students').

treatment.label: A one percent increase in all net-of-tax rates (1 - m_i) along the intensive margin

register_source.value: Effective marginal tax rate schedule of Kleven and Kreiner (2006) for Denmark 2006, applied to IDA hourly wage rates

definition.value: A small reform of the initial tax system in which the marginal tax rates are reduced to create a one percent increase in the net-of-tax rates 1 - m_i everywhere along the intensive margin, Delta m_i = -Delta(1 - m_i) = -0.01(1 - m_i) for i = 1,...,N-1, with the participation tax m_0 = (T_1 - T_0)/w_1 unchanged. Effective marginal tax rates are the empirical 2006 Danish tax function of Kleven and Kreiner (2006) - income taxes, indirect taxes and the marginal claw-back on benefits - deflated to 2005 and assigned to each hourly wage from DKK 90 to DKK 714 by multiplying the wage rate by median annual hours (1660 h).

timing.value: Comparison of the model's pre-reform and post-reform long run steady states; the initial system is the Danish 2006 tax system

outcome.label: Delta D / Delta M, the change in the excess burden relative to the mechanical change in tax revenue

register_source.value: Model-implied; no register variable

definition.value: The change in the dead-weight loss D (Eq. (9)) divided by the mechanical change in tax revenue Delta M = (1 - u) sum_i Delta T_i g_i (Eq. (18)), i.e. the change in government revenue before behavioural responses. For a tax reduction it measures the efficiency gain per dollar of mechanical revenue loss, and for a small reform it also equals the degree of self-financing.

timing.value: Long run steady state of the model; the estimation uses the one-year transition from 2005 to 2006 and the 2006 tax system

units.value: ratio: change in the dead-weight loss per unit of mechanical change in tax revenue (equivalently the degree of self-financing, reported as a share)

magnitude.interpretation: A marginal reduction in the marginal tax rates, financed by lump sum taxation, yields an efficiency gain of 0.94 per unit of mechanical tax revenue loss; for a small reform this also equals the degree of self-financing.

estimand.time_horizon: Long run steady state of the model; the estimation uses the one-year transition from 2005 to 2006 and the 2006 tax system

population.selection: Workplace-level sample drawn from IDA: private sector workplaces in Denmark with workers aged 18-65 in 2005, observed in a specific week of 2004, 2005 and 2006. Observations in the top percentile of the wage distribution (wage rates above DKK 714) are excluded and wage rates below DKK 90 are dropped. 126,400 workplaces remain. Students are removed.

identification.source_of_variation: No reform or experiment: the structural parameters are identified from cross-sectional variation across 126,400 Danish private-sector workplaces in 2005 in the number of stayers x_h out of n_h employees (the 2005-to-2006 separation rate), combined with the exogenous effective marginal tax schedule of the Danish 2006 tax system (Kleven and Kreiner, 2006) mapped onto workplace average hourly wage rates, and with the offered wage distribution P estimated from workers hired from non-employment. The authors state the analysis 'exploits only cross-sectional variation across individuals for identification'.

key_assumptions.assumption: Worker and firm components in the wage are independent, so that a workplace's average wage rate measures the firm wage component plus noise and can be used as the wage w_i of job i in the model
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted, not tested; the authors restate it in the concluding section as one of the two things 'the empirical identification relies on'. No balance or decomposition evidence is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The distribution of job opportunities (the offered wage distribution P and its domain) is exogenous: it is not affected by taxation or by workers' search behaviour
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted; footnote 11 states that P and its domain are exogenous and can only be observed for the existing w1. No test.

key_assumptions.assumption: All workers are identical: the underlying (offered) wage distribution is the same for every individual, so there is no ability heterogeneity
key_assumptions.supported_by: Conceded in the concluding section as 'the most heroic assumption of the model'; not relaxed or tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Workers are indifferent between the lowest wage job and non-employment, w1 - T1 = w0 - T0, which pins down the value of leisure/home production w0 = (1 - m0) w1 = 36.9
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed as an identifying restriction; the implied value DKK 36.9 per hour is reported but not validated externally.

formal.as_written: w1 − T1 ≥ w0 − T0 ... w1 − T1 = w0 − T0, which implies w0 = w1 − (T1 − T0) = (1 − m0) w1

key_assumptions.assumption: The mobility (search) effort cost function is isoelastic, c(s) = c0 s^(1+1/gamma)/(1+1/gamma)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed 'to identify the model' (Eq. (15)); no specification test of the cost function is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: No discounting, so only the long run steady state matters for welfare and for the evaluation of tax reforms
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a simplifying modelling assumption in Section 2; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Job destruction is exogenous and random, arriving at a constant Poisson rate delta that does not depend on the worker's search effort or wage
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a model primitive; probed indirectly by the alternative-q robustness in Table 4 and by removing closing plants in Table 5.

key_assumptions.assumption: The offered wage distribution P is identified by the distribution of firm-specific average wages of workers who entered firms in 2005 from non-employment in 2004, weighted by each firm's share of such hires
key_assumptions.supported_by: Follows Christensen et al. (2005); supported only by the model-consistent observation that the earned wage distribution stochastically dominates it (Fig. 2).

key_assumptions.assumption: Behaviour depends on taxation only through the marginal tax rates, so the effective marginal tax rate schedule is sufficient information for estimation and for the policy simulations
key_assumptions.supported_by: Derived from Eq. (7) of the model: search effort depends on taxes only via T_{i+1} - T_i = m_i (w_{i+1} - w_i).

key_assumptions.assumption: The simulated reforms change only the intensive-margin marginal tax rates m1,...,mN-1: T0, T1 and hence w1 and the participation tax m0 are held fixed, and the offered wage distribution and the estimated structural parameters are invariant to the reform (no general-equilibrium wage response)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 4 and footnote 11 as 'an analytical necessity'; no general-equilibrium check is performed.

definition.value: A small reform of the initial tax system in which the marginal tax rates are reduced to create a one percent increase in the net-of-tax rates 1 - m_i everywhere along the intensive margin, Delta m_i = -Delta(1 - m_i) = -0.01(1 - m_i) for i = 1,...,N-1, with the participation tax m_0 = (T_1 - T_0)/w_1 unchanged. definition.value: The change in the dead-weight loss D (Eq. (9)) divided by the mechanical change in tax revenue Delta M = (1 - u) sum_i Delta T_i g_i (Eq. claims.statement: A small reduction in all marginal tax rates along the intensive margin yields a change in the excess burden of taxation equal to 0.97 of the mechanical loss in tax revenue (Table 5, column 'm0 = 0.82').

treatment.label: A one percent increase in all net-of-tax rates (1 - m_i) along the intensive margin

register_source.value: Effective marginal tax rate schedule of Kleven and Kreiner (2006) for Denmark 2006, applied to IDA hourly wage rates

definition.value: A small reform of the initial tax system in which the marginal tax rates are reduced to create a one percent increase in the net-of-tax rates 1 - m_i everywhere along the intensive margin, Delta m_i = -Delta(1 - m_i) = -0.01(1 - m_i) for i = 1,...,N-1, with the participation tax m_0 = (T_1 - T_0)/w_1 unchanged. Effective marginal tax rates are the empirical 2006 Danish tax function of Kleven and Kreiner (2006) - income taxes, indirect taxes and the marginal claw-back on benefits - deflated to 2005 and assigned to each hourly wage from DKK 90 to DKK 714 by multiplying the wage rate by median annual hours (1660 h).

timing.value: Comparison of the model's pre-reform and post-reform long run steady states; the initial system is the Danish 2006 tax system

outcome.label: Delta D / Delta M, the change in the excess burden relative to the mechanical change in tax revenue

register_source.value: Model-implied; no register variable

definition.value: The change in the dead-weight loss D (Eq. (9)) divided by the mechanical change in tax revenue Delta M = (1 - u) sum_i Delta T_i g_i (Eq. (18)), i.e. the change in government revenue before behavioural responses. For a tax reduction it measures the efficiency gain per dollar of mechanical revenue loss, and for a small reform it also equals the degree of self-financing.

timing.value: Long run steady state of the model; the estimation uses the one-year transition from 2005 to 2006 and the 2006 tax system

units.value: ratio: change in the dead-weight loss per unit of mechanical change in tax revenue (equivalently the degree of self-financing, reported as a share)

magnitude.interpretation: A marginal reduction in the marginal tax rates, financed by lump sum taxation, yields an efficiency gain of 0.97 per unit of mechanical tax revenue loss; for a small reform this also equals the degree of self-financing.

population.selection: Workplace-level sample drawn from IDA: private sector workplaces in Denmark with workers aged 18-65 in 2005, observed in a specific week of 2004, 2005 and 2006. Observations in the top percentile of the wage distribution (wage rates above DKK 714) are excluded and wage rates below DKK 90 are dropped. 126,400 workplaces remain.

identification.source_of_variation: No reform or experiment: the structural parameters are identified from cross-sectional variation across 126,400 Danish private-sector workplaces in 2005 in the number of stayers x_h out of n_h employees (the 2005-to-2006 separation rate), combined with the exogenous effective marginal tax schedule of the Danish 2006 tax system (Kleven and Kreiner, 2006) mapped onto workplace average hourly wage rates, and with the offered wage distribution P estimated from workers hired from non-employment. The authors state the analysis 'exploits only cross-sectional variation across individuals for identification'.

key_assumptions.assumption: Worker and firm components in the wage are independent, so that a workplace's average wage rate measures the firm wage component plus noise and can be used as the wage w_i of job i in the model
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted, not tested; the authors restate it in the concluding section as one of the two things 'the empirical identification relies on'. No balance or decomposition evidence is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The distribution of job opportunities (the offered wage distribution P and its domain) is exogenous: it is not affected by taxation or by workers' search behaviour
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted; footnote 11 states that P and its domain are exogenous and can only be observed for the existing w1. No test.

key_assumptions.assumption: All workers are identical: the underlying (offered) wage distribution is the same for every individual, so there is no ability heterogeneity
key_assumptions.supported_by: Conceded in the concluding section as 'the most heroic assumption of the model'; not relaxed or tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Workers are indifferent between the lowest wage job and non-employment, w1 - T1 = w0 - T0, which pins down the value of leisure/home production w0 = (1 - m0) w1 = 36.9
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed as an identifying restriction; the implied value DKK 36.9 per hour is reported but not validated externally.

formal.as_written: w1 − T1 ≥ w0 − T0 ... w1 − T1 = w0 − T0, which implies w0 = w1 − (T1 − T0) = (1 − m0) w1

key_assumptions.assumption: The mobility (search) effort cost function is isoelastic, c(s) = c0 s^(1+1/gamma)/(1+1/gamma)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed 'to identify the model' (Eq. (15)); no specification test of the cost function is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: No discounting, so only the long run steady state matters for welfare and for the evaluation of tax reforms
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a simplifying modelling assumption in Section 2; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Job destruction is exogenous and random, arriving at a constant Poisson rate delta that does not depend on the worker's search effort or wage
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a model primitive; probed indirectly by the alternative-q robustness in Table 4 and by removing closing plants in Table 5.

key_assumptions.assumption: The offered wage distribution P is identified by the distribution of firm-specific average wages of workers who entered firms in 2005 from non-employment in 2004, weighted by each firm's share of such hires
key_assumptions.supported_by: Follows Christensen et al. (2005); supported only by the model-consistent observation that the earned wage distribution stochastically dominates it (Fig. 2).

key_assumptions.assumption: Behaviour depends on taxation only through the marginal tax rates, so the effective marginal tax rate schedule is sufficient information for estimation and for the policy simulations
key_assumptions.supported_by: Derived from Eq. (7) of the model: search effort depends on taxes only via T_{i+1} - T_i = m_i (w_{i+1} - w_i).

key_assumptions.assumption: The simulated reforms change only the intensive-margin marginal tax rates m1,...,mN-1: T0, T1 and hence w1 and the participation tax m0 are held fixed, and the offered wage distribution and the estimated structural parameters are invariant to the reform (no general-equilibrium wage response)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 4 and footnote 11 as 'an analytical necessity'; no general-equilibrium check is performed.

claims.statement: Replacing the existing Danish tax system along the intensive margin with a constant marginal tax rate m = 0.3 changes Delta Y / Y, the relative change in aggregate income by 0.193.

treatment.label: Replacing the existing Danish tax system T along the intensive margin with the alternative system T-hat(m) with constant marginal tax rate m = 0.3 above w_1

register_source.value: Effective marginal tax rate schedule of Kleven and Kreiner (2006) for Denmark 2006 as the pre-reform system

definition.value: T-hat_0(m) = T_0 and T-hat_1(m) = T_1 as in the existing system and T-hat_i(m) = T_1 + m (w_i - w_1) for i = 2,...,N: a tax system with the same participation tax as the existing one and a single constant marginal tax rate m on all wage levels above w_1. The authors read this as roughly a transition from a Scandinavian system with high marginal taxes to a system along the lines of low-tax OECD countries such as the United States.

timing.value: Comparison of the model's pre-reform (Danish 2006 system) and post-reform long run steady states

outcome.label: Delta Y / Y, the relative change in aggregate income

register_source.value: Model-implied; no register variable

definition.value: The post-reform minus pre-reform aggregate income from Eq. (13), divided by the pre-reform level: the proportional change in average earned labor market income between the two steady states.

timing.value: Long run steady state of the model; the estimation uses the one-year transition from 2005 to 2006 and the 2006 tax system

units.value: proportional change in aggregate income (0.193 = 19.3%, described in the text as 'almost 20%')

magnitude.interpretation: Aggregate income rises by almost 20% relative to the Scandinavian income level.

estimand.time_horizon: Long run steady state of the model; the estimation uses the one-year transition from 2005 to 2006 and the 2006 tax system

population.description: The representative worker of the estimated on-the-job search model, calibrated on the full population of workers and workplaces in Denmark 2004-2006: workers aged 18-65 employed in private sector workplaces in 2005, aggregated to 126,400 workplaces employing 1.4 million workers.
population.period: 2004-2006 (base year 2005; the 2006 Danish effective marginal tax schedule deflated to 2005)

individuals older than 50 (removed in one robustness specification)

population.selection: Workplace-level sample drawn from IDA: private sector workplaces in Denmark with workers aged 18-65 in 2005, observed in a specific week of 2004, 2005 and 2006. Observations in the top percentile of the wage distribution (wage rates above DKK 714) are excluded and wage rates below DKK 90 are dropped. 126,400 workplaces remain.

identification.source_of_variation: No reform or experiment: the structural parameters are identified from cross-sectional variation across 126,400 Danish private-sector workplaces in 2005 in the number of stayers x_h out of n_h employees (the 2005-to-2006 separation rate), combined with the exogenous effective marginal tax schedule of the Danish 2006 tax system (Kleven and Kreiner, 2006) mapped onto workplace average hourly wage rates, and with the offered wage distribution P estimated from workers hired from non-employment. The authors state the analysis 'exploits only cross-sectional variation across individuals for identification'.

key_assumptions.assumption: Worker and firm components in the wage are independent, so that a workplace's average wage rate measures the firm wage component plus noise and can be used as the wage w_i of job i in the model
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted, not tested; the authors restate it in the concluding section as one of the two things 'the empirical identification relies on'. No balance or decomposition evidence is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The distribution of job opportunities (the offered wage distribution P and its domain) is exogenous: it is not affected by taxation or by workers' search behaviour
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted; footnote 11 states that P and its domain are exogenous and can only be observed for the existing w1. No test.

key_assumptions.assumption: All workers are identical: the underlying (offered) wage distribution is the same for every individual, so there is no ability heterogeneity
key_assumptions.supported_by: Conceded in the concluding section as 'the most heroic assumption of the model'; not relaxed or tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Workers are indifferent between the lowest wage job and non-employment, w1 - T1 = w0 - T0, which pins down the value of leisure/home production w0 = (1 - m0) w1 = 36.9
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed as an identifying restriction; the implied value DKK 36.9 per hour is reported but not validated externally.

formal.as_written: w1 − T1 ≥ w0 − T0 ... w1 − T1 = w0 − T0, which implies w0 = w1 − (T1 − T0) = (1 − m0) w1

key_assumptions.assumption: The mobility (search) effort cost function is isoelastic, c(s) = c0 s^(1+1/gamma)/(1+1/gamma)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed 'to identify the model' (Eq. (15)); no specification test of the cost function is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: No discounting, so only the long run steady state matters for welfare and for the evaluation of tax reforms
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a simplifying modelling assumption in Section 2; not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Job destruction is exogenous and random, arriving at a constant Poisson rate delta that does not depend on the worker's search effort or wage
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a model primitive; probed indirectly by the alternative-q robustness in Table 4 and by removing closing plants in Table 5.

key_assumptions.assumption: The offered wage distribution P is identified by the distribution of firm-specific average wages of workers who entered firms in 2005 from non-employment in 2004, weighted by each firm's share of such hires
key_assumptions.supported_by: Follows Christensen et al. (2005); supported only by the model-consistent observation that the earned wage distribution stochastically dominates it (Fig. 2).

key_assumptions.assumption: Behaviour depends on taxation only through the marginal tax rates, so the effective marginal tax rate schedule is sufficient information for estimation and for the policy simulations
key_assumptions.supported_by: Derived from Eq. (7) of the model: search effort depends on taxes only via T_{i+1} - T_i = m_i (w_{i+1} - w_i).

key_assumptions.assumption: The simulated reforms change only the intensive-margin marginal tax rates m1,...,mN-1: T0, T1 and hence w1 and the participation tax m0 are held fixed, and the offered wage distribution and the estimated structural parameters are invariant to the reform (no general-equilibrium wage response)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 4 and footnote 11 as 'an analytical necessity'; no general-equilibrium check is performed.

The choice of the bottom cut-off wage rate w1 and of the participation tax m0

Students excluded; individuals older than 50 excluded (Table 5)

Workers with less than 1 year of work experience excluded

definition.value: T-hat_0(m) = T_0 and T-hat_1(m) = T_1 as in the existing system and T-hat_i(m) = T_1 + m (w_i - w_1) for i = 2,...,N: a tax system with the same participation tax as the existing one and a single constant marginal tax rate m on all wage levels above w_1. definition.value: Minus the change in the dead-weight loss of taxation, D = W-tilde - W - R (Eq. (9)), divided by initial aggregate income Y; equivalently Delta(W + R)/Y. Positive numbers are efficiency gains.

population.selection: Workplace-level sample drawn from IDA: private sector workplaces in Denmark with workers aged 18-65 in 2005, observed in a specific week of 2004, 2005 and 2006. identification.source_of_variation: No reform or experiment: the structural parameters are identified from cross-sectional variation across 126,400 Danish private-sector workplaces in 2005 in the number of stayers x_h out of n_h employees (the 2005-to-2006 separation rate), combined with the exogenous effective marginal tax schedule of the Danish 2006 tax system (Kleven and Kreiner, 2006) mapped onto workplace average hourly wage rates, and with the offered wage distribution P estimated from workers hired from non-employment. key_assumptions.assumption: Worker and firm components in the wage are independent, so that a workplace's average wage rate measures the firm wage component plus noise and can be used as the wage w_i of job i in the model
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted, not tested; the authors restate it in the concluding section as one of the two things 'the empirical identification relies on'. No balance or decomposition evidence is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The distribution of job opportunities (the offered wage distribution P and its domain) is exogenous: it is not affected by taxation or by workers' search behaviour
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted; footnote 11 states that P and its domain are exogenous and can only be observed for the existing w1. No test.

key_assumptions.assumption: All workers are identical: the underlying (offered) wage distribution is the same for every individual, so there is no ability heterogeneity
key_assumptions.supported_by: Conceded in the concluding section as 'the most heroic assumption of the model'; not relaxed or tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Workers are indifferent between the lowest wage job and non-employment, w1 - T1 = w0 - T0, which pins down the value of leisure/home production w0 = (1 - m0) w1 = 36.9
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed as an identifying restriction; the implied value DKK 36.9 per hour is reported but not validated externally.

formal.as_written: w1 − T1 ≥ w0 − T0 ... w1 − T1 = w0 − T0, which implies w0 = w1 − (T1 − T0) = (1 − m0) w1

key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed 'to identify the model' (Eq. (15)); no specification test of the cost function is reported.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a simplifying modelling assumption in Section 2; not tested.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a model primitive; probed indirectly by the alternative-q robustness in Table 4 and by removing closing plants in Table 5.

definition.value: A small reform of the initial tax system in which the marginal tax rates are reduced to create a one percent increase in the net-of-tax rates 1 - m_i everywhere along the intensive margin, Delta m_i = -Delta(1 - m_i) = -0.01(1 - m_i) for i = 1,...,N-1, with the participation tax m_0 = (T_1 - T_0)/w_1 unchanged. value.normalisation: Powers (2, 2 log) selected by the FRACPOLY routine in Stata; the bracketed terms are centred (at 5.1 and 4.1 respectively)

regressors: the correlation between w_WSR and w_IDA
target_designation.reasoning: The text introduces the exercise as estimating 'a relationship between the two wage variables for the workers with information about both measures'.

claims.statement: The overtime/part-time adjusted wage rate predicted from the WSR is lower than the IDA wage rate in most of the wage distribution, and larger than it at the bottom.

treatment.label: w_IDA, the IDA hourly wage rate

register_source.value: IDA (Integrated Database for Labour Market Research), Statistics Denmark; annual labor income from tax return data and annual hours from ATP

definition.value: Annual labor income (including mandatory pension fund payments) divided by annual hours; annual labor income is based on third-party reported tax return data, while annual hours are imputed from the payments to the mandatory pension fund ATP, so overtime is not accounted for and part-time hours are imprecisely measured.

outcome.label: the predicted (overtime/part-time adjusted) wage rate E(w_WSR | w_IDA)

register_source.value: Predicted from the Wage Statistics Register (WSR / Lonstatistikken) given the IDA hourly wage rate

definition.value: The fitted value of the fractional polynomial regression of the WSR hourly wage rate on the IDA hourly wage rate, imputed for every worker in the sample and then averaged within workplaces; plotted in Fig. 5 against the IDA wage together with a 45-degree line.

units.value: DKK per hour (the figure plots the predicted wage rate against the IDA wage rate with a 45-degree line)

magnitude.interpretation: The predicted wage rate is lower than the IDA wage rate in most of the wage distribution, which the authors read as consistent with the existence of overtime work; at the bottom of the distribution it is larger, which they read as the WSR data better capturing part-time work.

estimand.target_population: Workers in the 126,400 sample workplaces with both an IDA and a WSR hourly wage rate
estimand.time_horizon: 2005, cross-section

population.description: The workers in the 126,400 sample workplaces who have both an IDA hourly wage rate and a wage rate reported in the Wage Statistics Register: 60% of the 1.4 million workers with an observed IDA wage rate, reduced to 54% of the original worker sample after trimming.
population.period: 2004-2006 (base year 2005; the 2006 Danish effective marginal tax schedule deflated to 2005)
subgroups_defined: students (removed in one robustness specification)
individuals older than 50 (removed in one robustness specification)
workers with less than 1 year of work experience (removed in one robustness test)
closing plants, and closing plus downsizing plants (removed in robustness tests)
men
women
population.selection: Workers in the estimation-sample workplaces with both an IDA and a WSR wage rate; the top and bottom one percent of IDA wage observations are dropped, as are IDA wage rates deemed of low quality by Statistics Denmark, leaving 54% of the original sample of workers.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation: a cross-sectional association between two measures of the same worker's hourly wage rate, used to impute an overtime/part-time adjusted wage rate for the workers without a WSR observation.

key_assumptions.assumption: The WSR (Lonstatistikken) hourly wage rate, reported by employers and accounting explicitly for overtime and part-time work, is the better-measured wage rate; the IDA wage rate inherits measurement error from annual hours imputed from the ATP mandatory pension fund
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued in Section 5: annual labor income is well measured (third-party reported tax return data) but annual hours are not, since overtime is not accounted for and part-time hours are imprecise.

key_assumptions.assumption: The fitted relationship E(w_WSR | w_IDA), estimated on the workers who have both measures, extrapolates to the whole sample
key_assumptions.supported_by: Only 60% of the 1.4 million workers have a reported WSR wage, and trimming leaves 54% of the original worker sample; the paper notes the low coverage rate but does not test for selection.

implies_edges.from: has a reported WSR wage rate

key_assumptions.assumption: A fractional polynomial with the powers selected by the Stata FRACPOLY routine is a flexible enough functional form for the relationship between the two wage measures
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted as 'a very flexible way to estimate a relationship between two variables'; no specification test is reported.

threats_discussed: Low coverage of the WSR wage rate (60% of workers, 54% after trimming)
Measurement error in IDA annual hours (overtime not accounted for, part-time hours imprecise)
Some IDA wage rates are deemed of low quality by Statistics Denmark and are dropped
robustness_checks: The imputed adjusted wage rate is carried through the full structural estimation in Table 5, column 'Adjusted wage rate'
unresolved_confounders: Whether the workers with a reported WSR wage rate differ from those without is not examined

estimator.value: Fractional polynomial regression (the FRACPOLY routine in Stata) of the WSR hourly wage rate on the IDA hourly wage rate, estimated on the workers observed in both sources; the sample correlation between the two measures is also reported

sample_n.value: The workers with both measures: 60% of the 1.4 million workers with an observed IDA wage rate, reduced to 54% of the original worker sample after trimming; no exact count is printed

source_table.value: Figure 5 (Predicted wage rate), with the statement in the text of Section 5, p. 82

nodes: w_IDA, the IDA hourly wage rate
w_WSR, the WSR hourly wage rate
has a reported WSR wage rate

edges.from: has a reported WSR wage rate

ambiguities: Figure 5 prints no numerical values beyond its axes, and the text gives no gap in DKK, so no point estimate is recorded.
The sign is recorded as mixed because the predicted wage is below the IDA wage in most of the distribution but above it at the bottom.
